claim: Cataract is one of the most prevalent protein aggregation disorders.
source: Cataract is one of the most prevalent protein aggregation disorders and still the most common cause of vision loss worldwide.
evidence: This is a statement presented in the abstract as established fact about cataract prevalence.

claim: Cataract is still the most common cause of vision loss worldwide.
source: Cataract is one of the most prevalent protein aggregation disorders and still the most common cause of vision loss worldwide.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Lam et al., 2015 in the Introduction.

claim: The metabolically quiescent core region of the human lens lacks cellular or protein turnover.
source: The metabolically quiescent core region of the human lens lacks cellular or protein turnover; it has therefore evolved remarkable mechanisms to resist light-scattering protein aggregation for a lifetime.
evidence: This is supported by citations in the Introduction (Bloemendal et al., 2004; Wride, 2011).

claim: Myo-inositol suppresses aggregation of lens crystallins.
source: We now report that one such mechanism involves an unusually abundant lens metabolite, myo-inositol, suppressing aggregation of lens crystallins.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data in Figures 1-7.

claim: Myo-inositol is severely depleted in human cataractous lenses compared to age-matched controls.
source: Given recent metabolomic evidence that it is severely depleted in human cataractous lenses compared to age-matched controls, we suggest that maintaining or restoring healthy levels of myo-inositol in the lens may be a simple, safe, and globally accessible strategy to prevent or delay lens opacification due to age-onset cataract.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tsentalovich et al., 2015 and Yanshole et al., 2019 in the manuscript.

claim: Myo-inositol's primary target is the rate-limiting bimolecular step on the aggregation pathway.
source: Unlike many known chemical chaperones, myo-inositol's primary target was not the native, unfolded, or final aggregated states of the protein; rather, we propose that it was the rate-limiting bimolecular step on the aggregation pathway.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 6D and 7, showing concentration dependence and late-stage addition effects.

claim: Cataract disease afflicts tens of millions of people per year.
source: Cataract disease afflicts tens of millions of people per year and is the worldwide leading cause of blindness (Lam et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Lam et al., 2015.

claim: Cataract is caused by light-scattering aggregation of crystallin proteins in the lens.
source: The disease is caused by light-scattering aggregation of the extremely long-lived crystallin proteins in the lens (Bloemendal et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bloemendal et al., 2004.

claim: Crystallin aggregation is associated with accumulation of post-translational modifications including disulfide formation, UV- or metal-catalyzed Trp oxidation, deamidation, Asp isomerization, Lys derivatization, truncation, and various others.
source: This aggregation is associated with accumulation of post-translational modifications, including disulfide formation, UV- or metal-catalyzed Trp oxidation, deamidation, Asp isomerization, Lys derivatization, truncation, and various others (Hains and Truscott, 2007; Serebryany and King, 2014; Su et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hains and Truscott, 2007; Serebryany and King, 2014; Su et al., 2011.

claim: Most age-onset cataract forms in the oldest, nuclear (or core) region of the lens.
source: Most age-onset cataract forms in the oldest, nuclear (or core) region of the lens (Bloemendal et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bloemendal et al., 2004.

claim: The cells in the nuclear region of the lens lack all organelles and thus protein synthesis and degradation capacity.
source: The cells in this region lack all organelles and thus protein synthesis and degradation capacity, and lens crystallins comprise ~90% of their protein mass (Wride, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wride, 2011.

claim: Lens crystallins comprise ~90% of the protein mass in nuclear lens cells.
source: The cells in this region lack all organelles and thus protein synthesis and degradation capacity, and lens crystallins comprise ~90% of their protein mass (Wride, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wride, 2011.

claim: Human γD-crystallin has a Tm above 80 °C at neutral pH.
source: The most thermodynamically stable crystallin in humans is γD-crystallin (HγD), which, at neutral pH, has a Tm above 80 °C (Serebryany et al., 2018), resistance to 8 M urea (Kosinski-Collins and King, 2003), and unfolding half-life estimated to be on the order of decades (Mills-Henry et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Serebryany et al., 2018.

claim: Human γD-crystallin has resistance to 8 M urea.
source: The most thermodynamically stable crystallin in humans is γD-crystallin (HγD), which, at neutral pH, has a Tm above 80 °C (Serebryany et al., 2018), resistance to 8 M urea (Kosinski-Collins and King, 2003), and unfolding half-life estimated to be on the order of decades (Mills-Henry et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kosinski-Collins and King, 2003.

claim: Human γD-crystallin has an unfolding half-life estimated to be on the order of decades.
source: The most thermodynamically stable crystallin in humans is γD-crystallin (HγD), which, at neutral pH, has a Tm above 80 °C (Serebryany et al., 2018), resistance to 8 M urea (Kosinski-Collins and King, 2003), and unfolding half-life estimated to be on the order of decades (Mills-Henry et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mills-Henry et al., 2019.

claim: Human γD-crystallin is particularly abundant in the nuclear region of the lens.
source: It is particularly abundant in the nuclear region of the lens and enriched in insoluble aggregates (Su et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Su et al., 2011.

claim: Human γD-crystallin is enriched in insoluble aggregates.
source: It is particularly abundant in the nuclear region of the lens and enriched in insoluble aggregates (Su et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Su et al., 2011.

claim: Human γD-crystallin consists of two homologous intercalated double-Greek key domains.
source: HγD consists of two homologous intercalated double-Greek key domains.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about γD-crystallin.

claim: The N-terminal domain of human γD-crystallin is less stable and derives part of its stability from the domain interface.
source: The N-terminal domain is less stable and derives part of its stability from the domain interface (Mills-Henry et al., 2019; Serebryany and King, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mills-Henry et al., 2019 and Serebryany and King, 2014.

claim: Human γD-crystallin contains six Cys residues, four of which are buried in the core of the N-terminal domain.
source: All γ-crystallins are Cys-rich (Serebryany et al., 2021); thus, HγD contains six Cys residues, four of which are buried in the core of the N-terminal domain, yet there are no disulfides in the native state of the protein in vitro or in the young lens (Basak et al., 2003; Fan et al., 2015; Ramkumar et al., 2018; Serebryany et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Serebryany et al., 2021 and structural studies.

claim: There are no disulfides in the native state of human γD-crystallin in vitro or in the young lens.
source: All γ-crystallins are Cys-rich (Serebryany et al., 2021); thus, HγD contains six Cys residues, four of which are buried in the core of the N-terminal domain, yet there are no disulfides in the native state of the protein in vitro or in the young lens (Basak et al., 2003; Fan et al., 2015; Ramkumar et al., 2018; Serebryany et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Basak et al., 2003; Fan et al., 2015; Ramkumar et al., 2018; Serebryany et al., 2018.

claim: The W42Q variant and the congenital W42R produce similarly strong aggregation under physiologically relevant oxidizing conditions.
source: We have shown that the oxidation-mimicking W42Q variant and the congenital W42R produce similarly strong aggregation under physiologically relevant oxidizing conditions (Serebryany et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Serebryany et al., 2016b.

claim: W42Q and W130E aggregates do not stain with Thioflavin T, indicating they are not amyloid fibrils.
source: These neutral-pH HγD aggregates do not stain with Thioflavin T, indicating that they are not amyloid fibrils (Serebryany and King, 2015; Serebryany et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Serebryany and King, 2015 and Serebryany et al., 2016a.

claim: Electron microscopy of cataractous lens cytoplasm did not reveal any extended fibrillar structures.
source: This is consistent with electron microscopy of cataractous lens cytoplasm, which did not reveal any extended fibrillar structures (Costello et al., 2012; Metlapally et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Costello et al., 2012 and Metlapally et al., 2008.

claim: Solution turbidity is proportional to total mass for W42Q and W130E aggregates.
source: Fortunately, we have shown that solution turbidity is proportional to total mass for these aggregates (Serebryany and King, 2015) and that simple power laws relate the aggregation rate and lag time to protein concentration, such that all aggregation traces collapse onto a single master curve, where all points that map onto a given master-curve point have the same particle size distribution (Serebryany et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Serebryany and King, 2015.

claim: No preventative or therapeutic drugs against cataract have been approved to-date.
source: Despite intense research interest (Makley et al., 2015; Shanmugam et al., 2015; Zhao et al., 2015), no preventative or therapeutic drugs against cataract have been approved to-date, leaving surgery as the only treatment option.
evidence: This is a statement of current clinical practice, supported by citations to research efforts.

claim: Surgery is the only treatment option for cataract.
source: Despite intense research interest (Makley et al., 2015; Shanmugam et al., 2015; Zhao et al., 2015), no preventative or therapeutic drugs against cataract have been approved to-date, leaving surgery as the only treatment option.
evidence: This is a statement of current clinical practice.

claim: Delaying the age of onset of cataract by ~14% would cut the need for surgery by half by pushing the onset of blindness beyond the average lifespan.
source: Delaying the age of onset of the disease by ~14% would cut the need for surgery by half by pushing the onset of blindness beyond the average lifespan (WHO, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to WHO, 2014.

claim: A diffusion barrier that forms during middle age prevents almost all externally applied compounds from penetrating into the lens nucleus.
source: The lens is a tightly packed tissue, and a diffusion barrier that forms during middle age prevents almost all externally applied compounds from penetrating into the lens nucleus (Heikkinen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Heikkinen et al., 2019.

claim: Myo-inositol is unusually abundant in the lens.
source: Metabolomic analyses showed certain small metabolites to be unusually abundant in the lens, notably myo-inositol (Tomana et al., 1984; Tsentalovich et al., 2015) – which, however, is greatly depleted in cataractous lenses (Tsentalovich et al., 2015; Yanshole et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tomana et al., 1984 and Tsentalovich et al., 2015.

claim: Myo-inositol is greatly depleted in cataractous lenses.
source: Metabolomic analyses showed certain small metabolites to be unusually abundant in the lens, notably myo-inositol (Tomana et al., 1984; Tsentalovich et al., 2015) – which, however, is greatly depleted in cataractous lenses (Tsentalovich et al., 2015; Yanshole et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tsentalovich et al., 2015 and Yanshole et al., 2019.

claim: Myo-inositol acts as a kinetic inhibitor of the aggregation of the W42Q variant of human γD-crystallin.
source: We now report that myo-inositol (commonly referred to as just 'inositol', since it is the naturally prevalent isomer) acts as a kinetic inhibitor of the aggregation of the oxidation-mimicking, cataract-associated W42Q variant of human γD-crystallin, as well as other variants that aggregate under physiologically relevant oxidizing conditions.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data in Figures 1-7.

claim: Myo-inositol slows the aggregation rate even when added at a later stage in the aggregation process.
source: Notably, this compound slows the aggregation rate even when added at a later stage in the aggregation process.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 7.

claim: Myo-inositol inhibits the rate-limiting bimolecular step in the aggregation pathway and thereby indirectly disfavors the non-native disulfide bonds that stabilize the aggregation precursor.
source: We present evidence that inositol inhibits the rate-limiting bimolecular step in the aggregation pathway and thereby indirectly disfavors the non-native disulfide bonds that stabilize the aggregation precursor.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Myo-inositol permeates into the lens from the outside by both passive and active transport.
source: As one of the very few molecules known to permeate into the lens from the outside, by both passive and active transport (Cotlier, 1970; Diecke et al., 1995), myo-inositol therefore has the potential to become a safe, simple, and globally accessible treatment to prevent or delay loss of vision due to age-onset cataract disease.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cotlier, 1970 and Diecke et al., 1995.

claim: Myo-inositol suppresses aggregation of W42Q HγD in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Figure 1A shows a representative set of normalized turbidity traces demonstrating strong and dose-dependent suppression of turbidity development by myo-inositol.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The amount of residual protein in the clarified supernatant has a strong linear inverse correlation with end-point solution turbidity.
source: Consistent with prior studies (see above), the amount of residual protein in the clarified supernatant had a strong linear inverse correlation with end-point solution turbidity, suggesting that these compounds inhibited the aggregation process without changing aggregate shape or size.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The concentrations of compounds used in Figure 1B were not high enough to alter bulk solution properties.
source: The concentrations of compounds used here were not high enough to alter bulk solution properties (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by rheometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Myo-inositol had a significant effect on aggregation suppression in the physiological concentration range.
source: Notably, myo-inositol had a significant effect in the physiological concentration range.
evidence: This is demonstrated by data in Figure 1C showing effects at ~82 mM concentration.

claim: The estimated concentration of myo-inositol in the free water fraction of the healthy human lens is 82±22 mM.
source: Assuming a water content of ~60% and a total of ~50% of the water in a bound state, per a prior study (Heys et al., 2008), we arrive at an estimate of 82±22 mM myo-inositol in the free water fraction of the healthy human lens.
evidence: This is calculated from data in Tsentalovich et al., 2015 and Heys et al., 2008.

claim: At 82±22 mM concentration, myo-inositol suppressed the rate of turbidity development by ~35% and increased the lag time by a similar amount.
source: In this concentration range, myo-inositol already had a substantial effect in our assay, suppressing the rate of turbidity development by ~35% and increasing the lag time by a similar amount (Figure 1D), consistent with the 'master curve' relationships among maximum rate, lag time, and endpoint turbidity (Serebryany et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: Aggregation of low [W42Q] in the presence of high [WT] was suppressed by myo-inositol.
source: Figure 1E shows that aggregation of low [W42Q] in the presence of high [WT] was also suppressed by myo-inositol.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Myo-inositol suppressed aggregation of the W130Q variant.
source: The W130Q variant, which mimics oxidation of the cognate tryptophan in the C-terminal domain, was likewise rescued.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Myo-inositol suppressed aggregation of the wild-type N-terminal domain of HγD.
source: Inositol suppressed aggregation of the wild-type N-terminal domain of HγD ('N-only') like that of the other variants.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Aggregation of N-only and W130Q is entirely redox-dependent.
source: Aggregation of N-only and W130Q, like that of W42Q, was entirely redox-dependent (Figure 1—figure supplement 4), so the aggregation precursor conformations adopted by all these variants are likely kinetically trapped by non-native disulfide bonds.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The 1H-15N HSQC NMR spectra for WT and W42Q HγD with and without inositol were superimposable.
source: Yet, the NMR spectra for each protein with and without inositol were superimposable; the minor systematic shift with inositol does not indicate specific binding, only a change in the solvent environment due to addition of osmolyte (Iwaya et al., 2020).
evidence: This is demonstrated by NMR data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: There is no defined binding interaction between inositol and the native structure of HγD WT or W42Q.
source: In sum, we found no defined binding interaction between inositol and the native structure of HγD WT or W42Q.
evidence: This is based on NMR data shown in Figure 2A and B and chemical shift analysis in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Myo-inositol produced only very minor stabilization of HγD domains (up to ~1 °C at the highest concentration).
source: Only very minor stabilization was observed (up to ~1 °C at the highest [inositol]) – not sufficient to account for the aggregation suppression.
evidence: This is demonstrated by DSF data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: At 200 mM myo-inositol, the Amide I spectra of N-only at 25 °C with and without inositol overlapped.
source: Even at 200 mM [myo-inositol], the Amide I spectra of N-only at 25 °C with and without inositol overlapped, except for a very small feature at ~1690 cm–1 that could not be confidently assigned (Figure 2F), and the calculated secondary structure content under both conditions matched the PDB reference structure (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Raman spectroscopy data shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Inositol suppressed the emergence of a ~1620 cm–1 peak attributable to β-sheet-rich aggregates.
source: In this experiment, inositol clearly suppressed conformational change in the sample (Ganim et al., 2008), notably the emergence of a ~1620 cm–1 peak (Figure 2G), which was attributable to β-sheet-rich aggregates (Holzbaur et al., 1996).
evidence: This is demonstrated by thermal scanning Raman data shown in Figure 2G and H.

claim: Myo-inositol produced no qualitative change in the morphology of the aggregates.
source: Myo-inositol produced no qualitative change in the morphology of the aggregates.
evidence: This is based on TEM analysis shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: 100 mM myo-inositol decreased both the number and the length of extended aggregates.
source: (A, B, C) 100 mM myo-inositol decreased both the number and the length of extended aggregates, but 250 mM myo-inositol did not.
evidence: This is demonstrated by TEM morphometry data shown in Figure 4A, B, and C.

claim: 100 mM myo-inositol depleted the smallest globular aggregates and slightly increased the size of intermediate ones.
source: (D, E, F) 100 mM myo-inositol depleted the smallest globular aggregates, slightly increased the size of intermediate ones, and left the largest ones unchanged, but 250 mM myo-inositol reduced the size of the largest aggregates.
evidence: This is demonstrated by TEM morphometry data shown in Figure 4D, E, and F.

claim: 250 mM myo-inositol reduced the size of the largest aggregates.
source: (D, E, F) 100 mM myo-inositol depleted the smallest globular aggregates, slightly increased the size of intermediate ones, and left the largest ones unchanged, but 250 mM myo-inositol reduced the size of the largest aggregates.
evidence: This is demonstrated by TEM morphometry data shown in Figure 4D, E, and F.

claim: Aggregation at OxD 0.15–0.40 was OxD-dependent but always more strongly suppressed by inositol than in the fully oxidizing buffers.
source: As shown in Figure 5, aggregation at OxD 0.15–0.40 was OxD-dependent but always more strongly suppressed by inositol than in the fully oxidizing buffers (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Maximum aggregation rate suppression by 100 mM inositol in redox buffers (OxD 0.15-0.40) was 51% ± 2%.
source: Suppression of maximum aggregation rate did not vary significantly among this series of redox buffers; we observed maximum aggregation rate suppression of 51% ± 2% (mean ± S.E.M. for the six redox buffers), significantly greater than the 35% ± 3% obtained from the fully oxidizing buffers (Figure 1).
evidence: This is based on quantification of data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: At low OxD values, turbidity traces became visibly biphasic in the presence of 100 mM inositol.
source: In fact, low OxD combined with 100 mM inositol slowed early (but not late) aggregate assembly so much that turbidity traces became visibly biphasic (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: 200 mM inositol suppressed aggregation of the W42Q/C108S/C110S triple-mutant almost completely.
source: Under those conditions, 200 mM inositol suppressed aggregation of the triple-variant almost completely (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In mildly oxidizing buffers (OxD' 0.15 or 0.20), a clear shift in the redox state distribution was observed in the presence of inositol.
source: In the more mildly oxidizing buffers (OxD' 0.15 or 0.20), a clear shift in the redox state distribution was observed in the presence of inositol (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by PEGylation gel-shift data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Myo-inositol shifted the molecular population in bulk solution toward the reduced state, despite not being itself redox-active.
source: Thus, surprisingly, myo-inositol was able to shift the molecular population in bulk solution toward the reduced state, despite not being itself redox-active.
evidence: This is based on PEGylation gel-shift data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The concentration-dependence of W42Q aggregation rate is quadratic, indicating a bimolecular rate-limiting step.
source: We have previously shown that the concentration-dependence of W42Q aggregation rate is quadratic, indicating a bimolecular rate-limiting step (Serebryany et al., 2019; Serebryany and King, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Serebryany et al., 2019 and Serebryany and King, 2015.

claim: Myo-inositol decreased the pre-exponential factor in the concentration dependence of W42Q aggregation.
source: We observed both these effects in the [W42Q]-dependence experiment in Figure 6D.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 6D showing rightward shift in the curve.

claim: Myo-inositol increased the exponent of the concentration dependence power law for W42Q aggregation.
source: We observed both these effects in the [W42Q]-dependence experiment in Figure 6D.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 6D showing larger exponent (2.41 vs 2.10).

claim: When myo-inositol was added to already-turbid solutions, the rate of further turbidity development became substantially and reproducibly slower than the blank-buffer controls.
source: Nonetheless, when myo-inositol was added to the already-turbid solutions, the rate of further turbidity development became substantially and reproducibly slower than the blank-buffer controls.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Myo-inositol can serve as an aggregation suppressor even at a later stage in the aggregation process.
source: Thus, myo-inositol can still serve as an aggregation suppressor even at a later stage.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Natural chemical chaperones, including myo-inositol, are typically expected to stabilize the native state of a protein.
source: Natural chemical chaperones, including myo-inositol, are typically expected to stabilize the native state of a protein, either directly by binding it or indirectly by destabilizing the unfolded state (Beg et al., 2017; Clark et al., 2012; Dandage et al., 2015; Dong et al., 2019; Gault et al., 2018; Gupta et al., 2016; Morgan et al., 2019; Okiyoneda et al., 2013; Street et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing typical osmolyte behavior.

claim: Rat lenses have less myo-inositol but much more taurine than human lenses.
source: Thus, while human lenses are rich in myo-inositol, rat lenses have less myo-inositol but much more taurine, another potential chemical chaperone (Kinoshita et al., 1969; Yanshole et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kinoshita et al., 1969 and Yanshole et al., 2014.

claim: Fish lenses are relatively low in both myo-inositol and taurine but highly enriched in N-acetyl histidine.
source: Fish lenses are relatively low in both myo-inositol and taurine but highly enriched in N-acetyl histidine instead (Rhodes et al., 2010; Tsentalovich et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rhodes et al., 2010 and Tsentalovich et al., 2019.

claim: Myo-inositol readily enters the lens thanks to dedicated transporters.
source: Myo-inositol, which readily enters the lens thanks to dedicated transporters (Cotlier, 1970; Diecke et al., 1995), had previously been thought of as an osmotic regulator in the lens (Zhou et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cotlier, 1970 and Diecke et al., 1995.

claim: Myo-inositol has no observable binding site on the native structure of HγD.
source: We have shown that myo-inositol is a kinetic inhibitor of human γD-crystallin aggregation. It has no observable binding site on the native structure (Figure 2A and B) and only a very minor effect on protein stability (Figure 2C and D) or on the morphology of mature aggregates (Figure 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by NMR data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Myo-inositol has only a very minor effect on HγD protein stability.
source: We have shown that myo-inositol is a kinetic inhibitor of human γD-crystallin aggregation. It has no observable binding site on the native structure (Figure 2A and B) and only a very minor effect on protein stability (Figure 2C and D) or on the morphology of mature aggregates (Figure 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by DSF data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: Myo-inositol suppresses an aggregation precursor or early aggregate.
source: Yet, we found evidence that it suppresses an aggregation precursor or early aggregate (Figure 2G and H) and preferentially depletes small aggregates (Figure 4A and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Raman spectroscopy data shown in Figure 2G and H.

claim: Myo-inositol preferentially depletes small aggregates.
source: Yet, we found evidence that it suppresses an aggregation precursor or early aggregate (Figure 2G and H) and preferentially depletes small aggregates (Figure 4A and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TEM morphometry data shown in Figure 4A and D.

claim: Disfavoring the bimolecular interaction is expected to indirectly favor reduction and refolding of the misfolded monomeric aggregation precursor that is kinetically trapped by non-native disulfide bonding.
source: Disfavoring the bimolecular interaction is expected to indirectly favor reduction and refolding of the misfolded monomeric aggregation precursor that is kinetically trapped by non-native disulfide bonding – and this is what we observed (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This is based on the model in Figure 6C and supported by PEGylation data in Figure 6B.

claim: Myo-inositol synergized with the glutathione redox couple to suppress aggregation more strongly under mild-to-intermediate levels of oxidation.
source: While inositol was an effective aggregation suppressor even in fully oxidizing buffer (Figure 1), it synergized with the glutathione redox couple to suppress aggregation more strongly under mild-to-intermediate levels of oxidation (Figure 5 and Figure 6A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figures 5 and 6A.

claim: The aggregation process is misfolding-limited, not nucleation-limited.
source: We refer to the proposed target of inositol as a rate-limiting bimolecular interaction, rather than as a dimeric aggregation nucleus, because we have previously shown that the aggregation process is misfolding-limited, not nucleation-limited (Serebryany et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Serebryany et al., 2016b.

claim: A dimeric interaction may be the catalyst for non-native disulfide bonding, especially in redox buffers.
source: Thus, a dimeric interaction may be the catalyst for non-native disulfide bonding, especially in redox buffers, as indicated in Model 2 of Figure 6C.
evidence: This is based on prior atomistic modeling (Serebryany et al., 2016b) and the model shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Mature coalesced aggregates settle to the bottom of the reaction vessel during the course of the experiment.
source: We have previously observed that mature coalesced aggregates settle to the bottom of the reaction vessel during the course of the experiment (Serebryany and King, 2015; Serebryany et al., 2016a) – an effect that also occurred in the current study but did not significantly affect turbidity measurements due to the vertically oriented optics.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Serebryany and King, 2015 and Serebryany et al., 2016a.

claim: Continued rise in turbidity depends on continued formation and coalescence of new aggregate particles even as the soluble monomer is gradually depleted.
source: Then, continued rise in turbidity depends on continued formation and coalescence of new aggregate particles even as the soluble monomer is gradually depleted.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that aggregates settle and the model of aggregation kinetics.

claim: The microscopic rate-limiting bimolecular interaction determines the number of particles that can finally precipitate as large light-scattering globules.
source: Thus, the microscopic rate-limiting bimolecular interaction determines the number of particles that can finally precipitate as large light-scattering globules.
evidence: This is inferred from the aggregation kinetics and TEM morphometry data.

claim: Myo-inositol could be used to slow down cataract progression.
source: If this mechanism translates to the lens, myo-inositol could be used to slow down cataract progression.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the experimental findings.

claim: Redox chemistry plays a large role in βγ-crystallin aggregation.
source: For example, since redox chemistry plays a large role in βγ-crystallin aggregation (Serebryany et al., 2016b; Serebryany et al., 2018), and glutathione fails to diffuse into the aging lens (Lim et al., 2020), replacing one hydroxyl of myo-inositol with a thiol might yield a bifunctional anti-cataract drug – an aggregation suppressor and a reducing agent.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Serebryany et al., 2016b; Serebryany et al., 2018.

claim: Glutathione fails to diffuse into the aging lens.
source: For example, since redox chemistry plays a large role in βγ-crystallin aggregation (Serebryany et al., 2016b; Serebryany et al., 2018), and glutathione fails to diffuse into the aging lens (Lim et al., 2020), replacing one hydroxyl of myo-inositol with a thiol might yield a bifunctional anti-cataract drug – an aggregation suppressor and a reducing agent.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lim et al., 2020.

claim: One of the inositol transporters expressed in the lens (SMIT1) has been shown to import inositols modified with chlorine, fluorine, or azide in at least one position.
source: The inositol transporters expressed in the lens are quite selective, yet one of them (SMIT1) has been shown to import inositols modified with chlorine, fluorine, or azide in at least one position (Fenili et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fenili et al., 2011.

claim: Young lenses have a lower free water content than aged lenses.
source: The observation that young lenses have a lower free water content (Heys et al., 2008) suggests that effective [myo-inositol] is highest in young age.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Heys et al., 2008.

claim: A typical human diet is estimated to contain 1–2 g of myo-inositol per day.
source: A typical human diet is estimated to contain 1–2 g of myo-inositol per day, and ~4 g/day is produced endogenously from glucose in the liver and kidney (Fisher et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fisher et al., 2002.

claim: Approximately 4 g/day of myo-inositol is produced endogenously from glucose in the liver and kidney.
source: A typical human diet is estimated to contain 1–2 g of myo-inositol per day, and ~4 g/day is produced endogenously from glucose in the liver and kidney (Fisher et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fisher et al., 2002.

claim: The lens appears to have the highest myo-inositol levels of all human tissues studied.
source: Of all human tissues in which myo-inositol levels have been studied, the lens appears to have the highest, while the second-highest levels are found in the cytoplasm of neurons in the brain (Fisher et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fisher et al., 2002.

claim: The second-highest myo-inositol levels in human tissues are found in the cytoplasm of neurons in the brain.
source: Of all human tissues in which myo-inositol levels have been studied, the lens appears to have the highest, while the second-highest levels are found in the cytoplasm of neurons in the brain (Fisher et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fisher et al., 2002.

claim: High brain inositol has been ascribed to the need for signaling processes via second-messenger cascades.
source: High brain inositol has been ascribed to the need for signaling processes via second-messenger cascades (Fisher et al., 2002), but it may also act as a chemical chaperone there.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fisher et al., 2002.

claim: Myo- and scyllo-inositol, as well as some derivatives, have been shown to directly bind and stabilize oligomers of Aβ42, inhibiting amyloid aggregation.
source: Thus, both myo- and scyllo-inositol, as well as some derivatives, have been shown to directly bind and stabilize oligomers of Aβ42, inhibiting amyloid aggregation (McLaurin et al., 2000; Sun et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to McLaurin et al., 2000 and Sun et al., 2008.

claim: Scyllo-inositol has been clinically studied in Alzheimer's disease in humans, with some promise as a disease-modifying agent.
source: Scyllo-inositol has been clinically studied in Alzheimer's disease in humans, with some promise as a disease-modifying agent (Tariot et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tariot et al., 2012.

claim: In rats with streptozotocin- or galactose-induced cataracts, dietary supplementation with myo-inositol dramatically decreased the rate of cataract development.
source: Thus, in rats with streptozotocin- or galactose-induced cataracts, dietary supplementation with myo-inositol dramatically decreased the rate of cataract development: by 14 weeks of age, the untreated animals had totally opaque lenses, while the treated showed only initial stages of cataractogenesis (Beyer-Mears et al., 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Beyer-Mears et al., 1989.

claim: Dietary supplementation with myo-inositol triphosphate delayed cataract onset by ~44% in streptozotocin-induced diabetic rats.
source: In another study, dietary supplementation with myo-inositol triphosphate delayed cataract onset by ~44% in streptozotocin-induced diabetic rats (Ruf et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ruf et al., 1992.

claim: Genetic overexpression of the native lens myo-inositol transporter in mice resulted in cataract due to hyperosmotic stress.
source: Dosage of myo-inositol is likely to be important in any potential cataract treatments, as genetic overexpression of its native lens transporter in mice resulted in cataract due to hyperosmotic stress (Jiang et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jiang et al., 2000.

claim: Trisomy-21 (Down's syndrome) is associated with premature cataract.
source: Trisomy-21 (Down's syndrome), which leads to overexpression of the same transporter in humans, is likewise associated with premature cataract (Chhetri, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chhetri, 2019.

claim: Maintaining or restoring healthy levels of lens myo-inositol should be considered a promising strategy for delaying the onset of visual impairment or blindness due to cataract.
source: Given that myo-inositol is severely depleted in cataractous human lenses but not in age-matched controls (Tsentalovich et al., 2015; Yanshole et al., 2019), and given that it is one of the very few molecules able to permeate into lens tissue, maintaining or restoring healthy levels of lens myo-inositol should be considered a promising strategy for delaying the onset of visual impairment or blindness due to cataract and thus reducing the global burden of this highly prevalent disease.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the experimental findings and cited metabolomic studies.
